name: Thomas Cranmer
role: Archbishop of Canterbury (1533–1556), architect of the English Book of Common Prayer

died.cause: Burned at the stake for heresy

summary: Archbishop of Canterbury under Henry VIII and Edward VI who annulled Henry's first marriage, led the English Reformation's changes to worship, and wrote the Book of Common Prayer. Under Mary I he was tried for heresy, recanted, then withdrew his recantations and was burned.

key_dates.label: Proposes polling the universities on Henry VIII's annulment, entering royal service
Secretly marries Margarete, niece of the Lutheran reformer Andreas Osiander
Becomes Archbishop of Canterbury; declares Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon void
Writes the preface to the second edition of the Great Bible ("Cranmer's Bible")
Issues the English Litany, the first official service in English
Revised, more Protestant Book of Common Prayer
Forty-two Articles; arrested after Mary I's accession

accomplishments.text: Wrote and compiled the Book of Common Prayer (1549, revised 1552), putting all public worship into English. Its language has shaped English-speaking Christianity and the English language ever since.
As Archbishop of Canterbury, declared Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon void (1533) and later presided over the annulments of his marriages to Anne Boleyn (1536) and Anne of Cleves (1540).
Promoted the English Bible: he wrote the preface to the Great Bible (1540) and supported placing an English Bible in every parish church.
Drafted the Forty-two Articles (1553), the basis of the Church of England's Thirty-nine Articles, and contributed to the Book of Homilies (1547).
Invited Continental reformers such as Martin Bucer and Peter Martyr Vermigli to England.
Took part in heresy proceedings himself as archbishop, including the condemnation of John Frith (burned 1533) and of the Anabaptist Joan Bocher (burned 1550).
At his execution, withdrew the recantations he had signed and held his right hand, which had signed them, in the fire first.

original.reference: Collect for the Second Sunday in Advent, Book of Common Prayer (1549)
original.note: One of the collects (short prayers) that Cranmer composed new rather than translated.

popularized.reference: Marriage service, Book of Common Prayer (1549; originally "till death us depart")
popularized.note: English wedding vows were already used in the medieval Sarum rite; Cranmer's prayer book fixed this wording in the language.

popularized.phrase: "Earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust"
popularized.reference: Burial service, Book of Common Prayer (1549)
popularized.note: Adapted from the older Latin burial rite and Genesis 3:19, and made familiar through the prayer book.

persecution_note: When the Catholic Mary I became queen in 1553, Cranmer was imprisoned, convicted of treason, and then tried for heresy under papal authority. He signed a series of recantations, but was condemned to be burned anyway. At the stake he renounced the recantations.

persecution.title: Imprisoned in the Tower and convicted of treason
persecution.summary: Cranmer had signed Edward VI's plan to pass the crown to Lady Jane Grey. After Mary I took the throne, he was sent to the Tower of London, partly after he publicly denounced the restoration of the Mass, and was tried and condemned for treason with Lady Jane Grey.

responsible.name: Mary I
responsible.role: Queen of England; had him imprisoned and tried

persecution.outcome: Convicted of treason, but kept alive so that he could be tried for heresy.

persecution.title: Heresy disputation, trial, and degradation at Oxford
persecution.summary: Cranmer was moved to Oxford with Nicholas Ridley and Hugh Latimer, held in the Bocardo prison, and made to defend his views on the Eucharist in a public disputation (April 1554). After England was reconciled to Rome, he was tried for heresy in September 1555 before James Brooks, Bishop of Gloucester, acting as papal commissioner. He was made to watch from his prison as Ridley and Latimer were burned (October 1555). Pope Paul IV condemned him in December 1555, and in February 1556 he was formally degraded from his orders by Bishops Edmund Bonner and Thomas Thirlby.

responsible.name: Mary I
responsible.role: Queen of England; refused to spare him

responsible.name: Cardinal Reginald Pole
responsible.role: Papal legate in England; succeeded him as Archbishop of Canterbury

responsible.name: Pope Paul IV
responsible.role: Pronounced sentence against him in Rome

responsible.name: James Brooks
responsible.role: Bishop of Gloucester; presided at his heresy trial as papal commissioner

responsible.name: Edmund Bonner
responsible.role: Bishop of London; carried out his degradation

responsible.name: Thomas Thirlby
responsible.role: Bishop of Ely; carried out his degradation

persecution.outcome: Condemned as a heretic and handed over to the secular authorities.

persecution.title: Recantations, then burning
persecution.summary: In prison Cranmer signed several recantations accepting papal authority and Catholic doctrine. Under the law, a repentant heretic might be spared, but Mary refused. Brought to the University Church to read a final recantation, he instead renounced all his recantations and rejected the pope. He was taken to the place outside Balliol College where Ridley and Latimer had died and burned, putting his right hand into the flames first.

responsible.name: Mary I
responsible.role: Refused to pardon him despite his recantations

responsible.name: City and university authorities of Oxford

persecution.outcome: Burned on 21 March 1556. Cardinal Pole was consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury the next day.

excommunication_note: Cranmer was condemned by Pope Paul IV in 1555, deprived of his archbishopric, and handed over for execution after being degraded from his orders. The sentence was never lifted by Rome. He is commemorated as a reformer and martyr in the Church of England and the Anglican Communion.

excommunications.reason: Heresy and schism; deprived of the archbishopric of Canterbury
excommunications.status: Carried out by his degradation (February 1556) and execution; never lifted

persecuted_others_note: As archbishop, Cranmer took part in heresy proceedings that ended in burnings under both Henry VIII (John Frith, John Lambert, Anabaptists) and Edward VI (Joan Bocher, George van Parris), and helped deprive Catholic bishops under Edward. He was also known for interceding for others, urging that Thomas More and John Fisher be allowed a partial oath and writing to the king on behalf of Anne Boleyn and Thomas Cromwell, before he was himself burned under Mary I.

persecuted_others.title: Condemnation of John Frith
persecuted_others.targets: John Frith, evangelical scholar who denied the real presence in the Eucharist
persecuted_others.summary: Cranmer examined Frith at Croydon and, with Bishops John Stokesley and Stephen Gardiner, tried to persuade him to recant; when Frith refused he was condemned and burned at Smithfield on 4 July 1533. Cranmer described the case in a letter of the time; he later came to views on the Eucharist close to Frith's.

persecuted_others.title: Examination of Elizabeth Barton
persecuted_others.targets: Elizabeth Barton, the 'Holy Maid of Kent', a visionary who prophesied against Henry's divorce
persecuted_others.summary: Cranmer examined Barton in 1533 and obtained her confession that her revelations were feigned. She and several clergy who supported her were then condemned by act of attainder, without trial, and hanged at Tyburn in April 1534.

persecuted_others.title: Heresy trials of Anabaptists and of John Lambert
persecuted_others.targets: Dutch Anabaptists in England; John Lambert
persecuted_others.summary: Cranmer headed a royal commission against Anabaptists in 1538, after which some were burned. In November 1538 he was one of the bishops who disputed against John Lambert at the trial over which Henry VIII presided; Lambert, who denied the real presence, was condemned and burned.

persecuted_others.title: Deprivation of Catholic bishops
persecuted_others.targets: Bishops Edmund Bonner of London and Stephen Gardiner of Winchester
persecuted_others.summary: Cranmer sat on the royal commissions that deprived Bonner (1549) and Gardiner (1551) of their sees; both were imprisoned until Mary I's accession.

persecuted_others.title: Burnings of Joan Bocher and George van Parris
persecuted_others.targets: Joan Bocher, Anabaptist; George van Parris, Flemish surgeon who denied the divinity of Christ
persecuted_others.summary: Cranmer led the commissions that condemned Bocher (burned 2 May 1550) and van Parris (burned April 1551) for heresy. A later story in Foxe that Cranmer pressed a reluctant Edward VI to sign Bocher's warrant is doubted by historians, including Diarmaid MacCulloch.

persecuted_others.title: Reform of canon law (Reformatio legum ecclesiasticarum)
persecuted_others.summary: The draft revision of church law prepared under Cranmer's direction provided that heretics who would not recant should be handed over to the civil authorities for punishment. Parliament never enacted it.

sources.citation: The Book of Common Prayer: The Texts of 1549, 1559, and 1662, ed. Brian Cummings (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2011).
John Foxe, Acts and Monuments ("Foxe's Book of Martyrs"), 1563; enlarged ed. 1570. Account of Cranmer's trial and death.
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Thomas Cranmer: A Life (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1996).
